content: Hemophilia is diagnosed through a combination of screening tests and specific clotting factor tests. Screening tests are used to determine whether blood is clotting properly, while clotting factor tests identify the presence of hemophilia, its type, and its severity. Who Should Be Tested for Hemophilia? Families with a History of Hemophilia: If there is a family history of unusual bleeding, such as prolonged bleeding after surgery or injury, or unexplained deaths among male relatives (e.g., maternal uncles, grandfathers, or cousins), it is important to discuss this with a healthcare provider to evaluate the possibility of hemophilia. Physicians often take a detailed family history to assess the likelihood of a bleeding disorder. Certain newborns should be tested for hemophilia shortly after birth, including: Babies born into families with a known history of hemophilia. Babies whose mothers are carriers of the hemophilia gene. Babies who exhibit bleeding symptoms at birth. Testing umbilical cord blood is more effective in detecting low levels of factor VIII (associated with hemophilia A) than factor IX (associated with hemophilia B). This is because factor IX levels are naturally low at birth and do not reach normal levels until the baby is at least six months old. Therefore, mildly low factor IX levels at birth do not necessarily confirm hemophilia B, and repeat testing may be required as the child grows. Families Without a History of Hemophilia: Approximately one-third of babies diagnosed with hemophilia have no family history of the disorder. A physician may suspect hemophilia in a newborn if: Bleeding persists for an extended period after circumcision. Prolonged bleeding occurs after blood draws or heel sticks (used for newborn screening tests). Bleeding in the scalp or brain is observed following a difficult delivery or the use of delivery-assisting instruments (e.g., vacuum or forceps). The baby develops unusual or raised bruises, or an excessive number of bruises. If hemophilia is not diagnosed during the newborn period, parents may notice unusual bruising when the child begins to crawl or stand. Severe hemophilia often presents with significant bleeding issues early in life, leading to diagnosis within the first year. Milder forms of hemophilia may not be diagnosed until later in life. When Should Testing Be Performed? Individuals with a family history of hemophilia often request testing for their baby shortly after birth. Types of Tests for Hemophilia Diagnosis Screening Tests: Screening tests are blood tests that evaluate whether the blood is clotting properly. These include: 1. Complete Blood Count (CBC): This test measures hemoglobin levels, the size and number of red blood cells, and the number of white blood cells and platelets in the blood. While the CBC is often normal in individuals with hemophilia, prolonged or heavy bleeding can result in low hemoglobin and red blood cell counts. 2. Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (APTT) Test: This test measures the time it takes for blood to clot and evaluates the clotting ability of factors VIII, IX, XI, and XII. In individuals with hemophilia A or B, the APTT test will show a prolonged clotting time due to low levels of factors VIII or IX. 3. Prothrombin Time (PT) Test: This test also measures clotting time but primarily evaluates factors I, II, V, VII, and X. PT test results are typically normal in individuals with hemophilia A or B. 4. Fibrinogen Test: This test assesses the ability to form a blood clot and measures levels of fibrinogen (clotting factor I). It is often ordered alongside other clotting tests or when PT or APTT results are abnormal. Clotting Factor Tests: Clotting factor tests, also known as factor assays, measure the activity of clotting factors VIII and IX in the blood. These tests are essential for diagnosing hemophilia, determining its type (A or B), and assessing its severity. Knowing the type and severity of hemophilia is critical for developing an appropriate treatment plan. Hemophilia Severity Classification: The severity of hemophilia is determined by measuring baseline clotting factor activity before any treatment is administered. Results are expressed as a percentage of normal clotting factor levels, with the average normal level being 100% (normal range: 50%–150%). The International Society on Thrombosis and Hemostasis (ISTH) established the following classification in 2001: Mild Hemophilia: Clotting factor levels greater than 5% but less than 40%. Moderate Hemophilia: Clotting factor levels between 1% and 5%. Severe Hemophilia: Clotting factor levels less than 1%. Notes on Classification: The 2001 ISTH classification does not address individuals with clotting factor levels between 40% and 50%. However, some individuals in this range may experience bleeding symptoms. In 2021, ISTH introduced the terms symptomatic carrier (for individuals with clotting factor levels ≥40% and bleeding symptoms) and asymptomatic carrier (for those with clotting factor levels ≥40% but no bleeding symptoms). Women and girls with clotting factor levels below 40% are classified as having mild, moderate, or severe hemophilia based on their specific clotting factor levels.
